title: The video I mentioned:@Joe Weinberg #theatre #interactive #immersive ...
transcript: This ambitious piece of interactive theater is about spicy literature and censorship. And no, the irony is not lost on me that I have to be careful with my word choice on this app, just like the characters do in this play. When we enter the theater space, we explore a sort of museum exhibition about the censorship of literature along with writing prompts that explore some…intimate topics. When the play actually begins, it sort of takes the form of a mid-20th century spicy novel, but there's multiple meta layers to it where they incorporate some of our anonymous prompts into the storytelling and other sort of MadLib-esque details that the audience contributes along the way. And as it tells this archetypal story about liberation and awakening, we also learn some fascinating history about the harsh laws of that time and how authors tried to skirt them. I will say the various layers to the concept and the storytelling don't always mesh together as coherently as I might have liked. Some of it felt a little bit muddied and inconsistent to me. But I did genuinely appreciate the dramaturgical ambition to it. And more than that, I was just fascinated by this whole experience. It insightfully covers this subject matter that's rarely discussed in media and even brings us in on that experience through this interactive concept. I made a video recently, which i'll link in the caption, about a recent trend of theater pieces almost acting like health class for adults and alleviating some of our societal hangups around these topics. And this show definitely felt like it was continuing that trend. So if you're interested, after multiple successful extensions, Dirty Books is currently selling only through February 28th via Bated Breath Theatre Company
classificationReason: Creator clearly attended an immersive/interactive off-Broadway show about the censorship of 'spicy literature,' with a museum-exhibition entry, anonymous audience writing prompts, MadLib-style contributions, and a mid-20th century novel framing — all hallmarks of Dirty Books.
